strengths: The paper proposes a clear and intuitively appealing physical representation: learning low-dimensional force fields over object states and integrating them with an ODE solver rather than predicting trajectories entirely in latent space.
The problem setting is relevant and timely, targeting few-shot physical dynamics, out-of-distribution generalization, and planning rather than only short-horizon prediction.

Experiments cover two qualitatively different domains, I-PHYRE rigid-body puzzles and N-body gravitational dynamics, and include prediction, planning, and some ablations on integration precision and latent dimensionality.
The qualitative visualizations of learned forces and controlled force-response plots help support the interpretability claim and make the approach easier to understand.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited relative to prior work on graph neural physics simulators, neural ODEs, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian neural networks, neural operators, and force-based dynamics models. The paper does not sufficiently position NFF against the closest physics-informed continuous-time baselines.

The evaluation uses weak or incomplete baselines. IN and SlotFormer are useful references, but the absence of Neural ODE/GNN variants, HNN/LNN/SymODEN-style methods, Graph Network Simulator-type baselines, EGNN/equivariant dynamics models, or oracle/analytic force baselines makes the claimed advantage hard to calibrate.

Several central claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly invokes human-like few-shot learning and generalized physical principles, but the evidence is limited to symbolic-state simulations with 100 I-PHYRE trajectories or 200 N-body trajectories and thousands of training epochs.

The method description is underspecified in important places: object graph construction, neighbor definitions, handling of contacts/collisions/discontinuities, action encoding, segmentation during autoregressive training, and the precise ODE/state update are not detailed enough for confident reproduction.

The backward planning argument is technically questionable. The paper treats the learned ODE integration as invertible, but many target domains include friction, collisions, support/contact events, object removal, and other irreversible or discontinuous dynamics. This undermines the claimed analytical reverse-time planning capability.

Quantitative prediction results are mainly presented as plots without detailed numeric tables, making it difficult to assess effect sizes, statistical reliability, and whether improvements are consistent across scenarios and seeds.

The I-PHYRE planning comparison may conflate model quality with the search/refinement procedure. NFF evaluates 500 random action candidates and updates after failures, but the fairness and computational budget relative to baselines are not fully established.

The force-field representation absorbs masses and other constants into learned forces, which may hurt extrapolation to different masses or physical regimes; the paper does not sufficiently test such systematic generalization.

The scope is narrower than the framing suggests: the approach assumes clean symbolic object states and does not address perception, partial observability, noisy tracking, or real-world data, yet the introduction and conclusion make broad claims about physical reasoning agents.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are helpful but still insufficient, and there is no clear mention of released code, trained models, exact splits, or scripts to regenerate the datasets and planning results.

strengths: The paper proposes a physically motivated inductive bias: representing object interactions as low-dimensional force fields and integrating them with an ODE solver. This is a sensible direction for sample-efficient physical dynamics learning.
The evaluation attempts to cover both short-range contact-rich dynamics in I-PHYRE and long-range gravitational dynamics in N-body simulations, including prediction and planning settings.

The qualitative force visualizations and controlled force-response probes are potentially useful for interpretability, and the paper includes some ablations on integrator choice, step size, and latent dimensionality.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited and not well positioned against prior physics-informed and graph-based dynamics models. The method appears close to existing graph neural simulators, neural ODEs, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian neural networks, and neural operator-style interaction models, but the paper does not make a convincing case for a distinct technical advance.

The technical formulation is underspecified and sometimes physically questionable. Collision, support, friction, springs, constraints, discontinuous object deletion, and rotational effects are all claimed to be handled by a unified smooth learned force field, but the paper gives little detail on how these are represented, integrated, or made stable. Mass is simply absorbed into the learned force, which weakens the claim of learning general physical principles.

The empirical comparison is too narrow for the strength of the claims. The main baselines are IN and SlotFormer, while many relevant alternatives are missing, including stronger graph network simulators, neural relational inference variants, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian/symplectic models, equivariant GNNs for N-body systems, and task-specific I-PHYRE agents or planners.

The evaluation design raises fairness concerns. Hyperparameters and batch sizes differ between NFF and baselines, there is little evidence of careful baseline tuning, and the planning comparisons confound model quality with random action sampling, refinement protocol, and candidate selection. The N-body backward-planning result strongly favors a reversible ODE-style model, so the comparison to feedforward baselines is not very informative.

The few-shot and OOD claims are overstated. Training on 100 I-PHYRE trajectories of 150 timesteps and 200 N-body trajectories is not clearly 'a few examples,' and the N-body task may largely reduce to learning a simple gravitational law in symbolic state space. The paper does not test broader transfer to new object types, unseen force laws, varying masses in I-PHYRE, perception input, or real-world data.

Quantitative reporting is weak. Many key results are shown only in plots without numeric tables, confidence intervals are limited, statistical tests are absent, and details such as dataset splits, random seeds, tuning budgets, failure modes, and exact planning protocols are insufficient for confident assessment.

Reproducibility is limited. The paper gives some hyperparameters, but omits enough architectural, implementation, and preprocessing detail that reproducing the symbolic state construction, graph neighborhoods, action/refinement loop, and force visualizations would be difficult.

The presentation contains notable polish issues, including 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size,' typos, malformed symbols/glyphs in the appendix, and several broad claims such as 'human-like' physical reasoning and 'interpretable force fields' that are not adequately substantiated.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: sample-efficient physical reasoning and OOD generalization from limited interaction data.

The Neural Force Field formulation is intuitive and appealing: representing interactions as low-dimensional force fields and integrating them with an ODE solver gives the model a useful physical inductive bias and some interpretability.

The empirical scope is stronger than many papers in this area, covering both I-PHYRE rigid-body interaction tasks and N-body gravitational dynamics, with within-scenario, cross-scenario, planning, and ablation evaluations.
Results are consistently favorable across prediction and planning settings, especially on cross-scenario N-body and I-PHYRE planning, where NFF substantially outperforms IN and SlotFormer baselines.
The ablations on integration step size, ODE grounding, integration method, and latent dimensionality support the main architectural choices and help explain why the approach works.
The force-response visualizations are a nice qualitative contribution, making the learned representation more interpretable than standard latent dynamics models.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but not decisive: the approach combines established ideas from graph interaction models, neural operators/DeepONets, Neural ODEs, and physics-informed dynamics. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning against Hamiltonian/Lagrangian neural networks, graph network simulators, Neural Relational Inference-style models, and other physics-inspired simulators.

The baseline set is somewhat narrow. IN and SlotFormer are useful, but the claims about general physical reasoning would be stronger with comparisons to more recent graph-based physical simulators, equivariant dynamics models, or energy/constraint-aware neural ODE methods.

The evaluation uses symbolic/object-state inputs rather than perception, which is acknowledged but still limits the scope of the physical reasoning claims. The method may depend heavily on clean object states, known graph structure, and simulator-provided quantities.

Some central claims are stronger than the evidence. Phrases such as human-like few-shot learning and learning fundamental physical concepts are only partially supported; the experiments show useful generalization in controlled simulators, not broad human-level physical reasoning.

The few-shot framing is a bit stretched: I-PHYRE training uses 10 games with 10 trajectories each, and N-body uses 200 trajectories. This is sample-efficient relative to large-scale training, but not necessarily few-shot in the strict sense.

Planning comparisons are promising but somewhat confounded. NFF evaluates 500 sampled actions and refines after execution; it is not fully clear whether all baselines have equally strong planning/search budgets and adaptation procedures, or whether dynamics quality and planner design are cleanly separated.

Quantitative prediction results are mostly shown as plots rather than tables, making exact effect sizes, variance, and statistical significance harder to assess. More numerical reporting would improve reproducibility and confidence.

The ODE formulation is physically elegant, but collision/contact dynamics are discontinuous and constraint-heavy; the paper does not fully analyze when the smooth force-field/ODE approximation breaks down.

Reproducibility details are partial: hyperparameters and datasets are described, but the review version does not clearly indicate code release, implementation details for graph construction/action encoding, or enough planner details to reproduce all results.
Presentation is generally clear but has minor polish issues, including title-suppression artifacts, some typos, and occasional overclaiming in the narrative.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful inductive bias for physical reasoning: representing object interactions as explicit learned force fields and integrating them with an ODE solver. This is intuitive, interpretable, and well matched to the target domains.

The empirical scope is broad, covering state-based I-PHYRE, N-body dynamics, and vision-based PHYRE, with both prediction and planning evaluations. The reported gains over IN, GCN, SlotFormer, RPIN, and DQN are often substantial, especially in cross-scenario generalization.

The paper includes meaningful ablations on ODE grounding, neural-operator force prediction, and integration precision, which support the claim that the main design components contribute to performance.

The planning results are a strong point: NFF is used not only as a predictor but also as a learned simulator for forward/refinement-based planning and backward planning, with large reported gains in N-body initial-condition reconstruction and I-PHYRE interactive planning.
The learned-force visualizations and controlled force-response analyses make the model behavior more interpretable than standard latent transition models.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than clearly high. The method combines known ingredients: graph interaction models, neural operators/DeepONet, and neural ODE-style integration. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning against prior continuous-time relational dynamics, graph neural ODEs, neural fields, and physics-informed simulators.

Some central claims are overstated. Terms such as “human-like few-shot learning,” “fundamental physical concepts,” and “generalized physical reasoning” are stronger than the evidence supports, especially since the experiments remain in relatively constrained 2D/3D simulated rigid-body settings.

The few-shot framing is uneven. I-PHYRE uses 100 trajectories and N-body uses 200 trajectories, while PHYRE uses 12,000 trajectories plus segmentation masks and a pretrained TimeSFormer classifier for planning. This is much less data than some baselines, but not uniformly a few-shot setting.

The fairness of baseline comparisons is not fully established. It is unclear whether baselines were tuned equally for the low-data regime, whether they had comparable state/perception inputs, and how much of the PHYRE planning gain comes from NFF dynamics versus the pretrained classifier and action-selection pipeline.

The technical formulation is somewhat hand-wavy around difficult physical events. Contact, friction, collision discontinuities, object elimination, springs/joints, torques, and mass effects are folded into learned forces with limited formal detail. The claim of invertible backward planning is also questionable for dissipative dynamics, contacts, and interventions.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time. The checklist says code and data will be released after publication, which does not provide a current reproducibility path. Some implementation details are provided, but not enough to independently verify all baselines, planning procedures, and vision-based preprocessing.

The limitations section is too brief relative to the ambition of the claims. Important issues such as stochasticity, sim-to-real transfer, soft bodies/fluids, sensitivity to state-estimation errors, scaling with object count, and robustness under distribution shifts beyond template changes are not deeply analyzed.

strengths: The paper tackles an important problem: sample-efficient physical reasoning and generalization to unseen physical configurations, which is highly relevant for AI agents and world models.

The high-level idea of representing dynamics through explicit learned force fields integrated by an ODE solver is intuitive and potentially useful, especially for long-horizon trajectory prediction and planning.
The empirical scope is broader than many papers in this area, covering I-PHYRE, N-body dynamics, and PHYRE, with both prediction and planning evaluations.

The reported numbers are often substantially better than the selected baselines, especially in cross-scenario N-body prediction and I-PHYRE planning, suggesting that the physical inductive bias may be beneficial.
The paper includes some ablations on integration precision, ODE grounding, and the neural-operator component, plus appendices with training details and noise robustness experiments.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The method largely combines established ideas: graph-based interaction models, neural ODE integration, learned force/acceleration predictors, and DeepONet-style neural operators. The paper does not clearly distinguish NFF from prior graph neural ODE, neural relational inference, graph network simulator, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian/ODE-based physical dynamics, or force-field learning work.

The technical formulation is underdeveloped and sometimes physically questionable. For example, mass is said to be safely absorbed into the learned force field, which blurs force and acceleration and weakens the claim that the representation learns physically meaningful force fields, especially in variable-mass settings such as N-body.

The central claim of learning general physical principles is not convincingly established. The visualized force fields are qualitative, and there is no rigorous test of whether the learned forces correspond to true forces, obey invariances/conservation laws where appropriate, or extrapolate outside the training distribution in a physically interpretable way.

The baseline set is incomplete for the paper’s claims. Important comparisons to modern continuous-time graph dynamics models, graph neural ODEs, neural relational inference variants, graph network simulators, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian neural networks, EGODE-like models, and strong PHYRE-specific methods are missing or insufficiently discussed.

The evaluation may be unfair or difficult to interpret. Some baselines appear poorly matched to the proposed model’s state supervision and physical inductive biases, while the PHYRE setting uses object masks, velocities, sparse convolutions, and a pretrained TimeSFormer classifier; the contribution of each component is not isolated.

The few-shot framing is overstated. I-PHYRE and N-body use limited trajectories, but PHYRE uses 12,000 trajectories plus segmentation masks and velocity information. Calling the overall framework human-like few-shot physical reasoning is stronger than the evidence supports.

The planning experiments are not fully convincing. I-PHYRE planning uses 500 sampled action candidates and repeated refinement, but the role of search budget, action proposal distribution, simulator feedback, and model update schedule is not analyzed. N-body backward planning relies on an asserted invertibility of the learned ODE, but learned dissipative/contact dynamics are generally not reliably invertible.

The paper’s reproducibility is weaker than claimed. The checklist says code and data will be released after publication, which does not provide an immediate reproducibility path. Several details needed for exact replication, baseline tuning, random seeds, and model selection are either absent or scattered.

The statistical reporting is limited. Error bars are mostly SEM over trials or samples, but it is unclear whether variability across training seeds, data splits, and hyperparameter choices is included. Given the small-data claims, seed sensitivity is important.

The writing repeatedly makes broad claims such as human-like reasoning, physical principles, and interpretable force fields without enough evidence. The limitations section is brief and does not adequately address scaling, stochasticity, soft bodies, discontinuous contacts, identifiability of forces from trajectories, or dependence on privileged object/state information.

strengths: The paper proposes an appealing force-field representation for few-shot physical dynamics, combining neural operator-style force prediction with ODE integration. This is a clean inductive bias for the target domain and gives the method useful interpretability through explicit forces.
The empirical results are broad for a single paper: I-PHYRE, N-body, and PHYRE; prediction and planning; within- and cross-scenario settings; state-based and vision-based variants.

Reported gains over IN, GCN, RPIN, and SlotFormer are substantial, especially in cross-scenario N-body and PHYRE planning, and the paper includes useful ablations on ODE grounding, integration precision, and DeepONet/NOL.

The appendices provide many important details: dataset generation, hyperparameters, integration comparisons, noise robustness, planning times, and detailed I-PHYRE planning results. The qualitative force visualizations are also informative.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than clearly high. The method combines known ingredients: graph interaction models, neural fields/operators, and neural ODE-style integration. The paper would benefit from sharper positioning against latent/neural field discovery, graph neural ODEs, differentiable physics, and model-based planning methods.

Some comparisons raise fairness questions. The PHYRE table compares NFF trained on 0.012M trajectories to older baselines trained on very different data budgets and pipelines, while NFF also uses segmentation masks and a pretrained TimeSFormer classifier for planning. It is not fully clear that the baseline setup isolates the contribution of the proposed dynamics model.

The evaluation relies heavily on deterministic rigid-body simulators with strong state/mask supervision and often known object structure. The claims about human-like physical reasoning and broad physical principle abstraction are stronger than what the experiments support.

Important implementation details remain under-specified for reproducibility and interpretation, such as how neighbor/contact/attraction graphs are constructed, how action features enter the force model, whether any privileged simulator information is used, and how baselines are tuned under the same compute and data constraints. Code is only promised after publication.

The planning results are promising but not fully convincing as evidence of superior reasoning. I-PHYRE uses random candidate sampling plus online refinement, N-body planning exploits the invertibility of the chosen formulation, and comparisons to stronger model-based planners, differentiable simulation baselines, or oracle/physics-engine planners are missing.

The force-field learning claim is mostly qualitative except for selected visualizations; there is limited quantitative validation that the learned forces match true forces across interactions, especially for collisions, friction, springs, and vision-based PHYRE.

Limitations are acknowledged but narrow. The method may struggle with variable friction/elasticity, stochasticity, deformable objects, fluids, perception errors, and scaling to richer 3D scenes; these are central to the broad claims but not substantially evaluated.
